Projectile spawning: engagement.py

This module is the “we fired a thing” layer. It doesn’t do physics itself; it calls physics simulators and writes the resulting trajectories into the runtime buffers.

engagement

Bullets

spawn_burst(plane_pos, plane_vel, bullets=N, muzzle_speed=...)

Repeats pos/vel N times

Adds a small random angular spread (~2 degrees in radians) so bullet streams aren’t laser-perfect

Calls simulate_bullet_trajectory(...)

Adds the x/y/z trajectories to RUNTIME.active_bullets as float32

There’s also spawn_bullets(...) as a legacy wrapper for older call sites.

engagement

Rockets & bombs

spawn_rocket() and spawn_bomb() pull from RUNTIME.flight.plane_pos and .plane_vel, simulate trajectories, and add to the corresponding buffer.

Per-tick update

step_projectiles() simply calls .step() on all three projectile buffers.



So the intended loop is something like:

maybe spawn new projectiles this frame

step buffers

render projectiles at their new sample indices

check hits

(Exact ordering depends on how the rest of your app is wired, but this is the implied machinery.)

Hit detection against the player: aircraft_hits.py

This file is a focused “did the player get hit?” check for rockets and (optionally) bombs.

aircraft_hits

The collision method: segment-to-point distance

For each active projectile:

take the segment between the previous sample and the current sample (p0 → p1)

compute the closest point on that segment to the aircraft position

declare a hit if distance² ≤ radius²

This is a good compromise between:

“check only current sample” (can miss fast projectiles),

and full continuous collision detection (heavier).

Important safety valve: minimum sample index

Hits only count if sample_index >= min_sample:

rockets require at least 2 samples

bombs require at least 6 samples

This prevents self-hits near the moment of firing/spawn.

aircraft_hits

Effects of a hit

Removes hit projectiles from the buffer (buffer.remove(rows[hits]))

Spawns an explosion

Records an impact into RUNTIME.impacts

Optional debug print if WARBITS_IMPACT_DEBUG is enabled

Bomb hits are gated behind env var WARBITS_AIRCRAFT_BOMB_HITS (so bombs can be “cinematic only” unless turned on).

Enemy bogie system: enemy_bogies.py

This is both AI-ish movement and post-hit “death choreography” (tumble → parachute → crash).

enemy_bogies

How bogie motion is represented

Instead of integrating position per frame, it precomputes arrays:

_bog_x, _bog_y, _bog_z: float64 arrays sized to the total number of flight frames

Before it “appears,” those entries are NaN

get_position(frame) returns None if that frame is NaN

So bogie motion is basically: “a timeline array with gaps.”

enemy_bogies

Initialization and configuration

init(ax, flight_x, flight_y, flight_z, slice_map, ...) calls:

set_flight_path(...) to store the player flight path arrays and allocate bogie arrays

configure(...) to decide when/where the bogie appears and how it follows

configure(...) is doing some careful stuff:

If appear_at isn’t provided, it defaults near the end of the Escape phase (escape_end - 20), otherwise near the end of the whole run.

It computes an offset so the bogie stays roughly _SEPARATION_DISTANCE away from the player (in XY).

It computes a spawn point that’s outside the terrain bounds by a _SPAWN_MARGIN in the “direction away from the aircraft,” so it comes in from off-screen.

It enforces terrain clearance using sample_height(...) + _BOGIE_TERRAIN_CLEARANCE.

It fills the bogie arrays from appear_at onward by moving toward the offset target each frame using a “closing factor” (default _CLOSING_FACTOR).

Also, you can set hit_frame to force a deterministic hit at a specific frame (useful for scripted scenarios / testing).

enemy_bogies

Per-frame update(frame)

This does three main things:

Lazy mesh creation (only once it needs to render)

creates a bogie mesh via create_bogie_model(...)

attaches it to the axes

Normal flight behavior

keeps altitude above terrain clearance

updates mesh orientation using delta from previous frame as a “velocity-ish” direction vector

Hit logic

either:

triggers at _hit_frame_override, OR

checks for projectile hits (bullets/rockets/bombs) using the same segment-distance concept

When hit:

sets _bogie_hit = True, stores origin, resets fall tick counters

spawns an explosion at the bogie position

records an impact event

Post-hit fall sequence

Once hit, instead of following the path:

it drifts in a spiral-ish way using sin/cos of tick

it falls under constant acceleration using _BOGIE_FALL_SPEED and _BOGIE_FALL_GRAVITY, with dt derived from _cfg.SIM_DT_MS

spawns a parachute once

when it hits the ground or exceeds max fall time:

spawns explosion at ground

removes the mesh

marks destroyed

NaNs the rest of the timeline

So this module is a combined:

spawn planner

follower

hit detector

death animator

renderer hook
all in one.

enemy_bogies

Ground AAA emplacements: enemy_ground.py

This is the ground enemy system with:

simple geometry,

movement AI (patrol/engage/evade),

turret rotation,

hit checks,

and a small targeting API.

enemy_ground

Geometry model

Each emplacement is a couple of boxes:

base box (bigger)

turret box (smaller)

Faces are stored as NumPy float32 arrays for fast rotate + translate.



Rotation is around Z only (_rotate_faces_z), i.e., the turret “spins” to face the aircraft’s XY position.

enemy_ground

Runtime state & initialization

Global _cols: list of Poly3DCollection (currently exactly two collections)

Global _emplacements: list of _Emplacement dataclass instances holding:

faces, center position, home position, velocity, mode, etc.

init(ax) creates those two Poly3DCollections and adds them to the axes. It also builds two _Emplacement objects if none exist.



reset():

picks spawn placements inside bounds,

jitters them,

seeds patrol targets,

clears destroyed flags and makes collections visible again.

enemy_ground

Movement AI (_advance)

Each frame, each live emplacement chooses a mode based on distance to target (aircraft XY):

patrol: wander around a patrol target, sometimes orbiting

engage: orbit around the aircraft at an engage orbit radius

evade: run away-ish with some perpendicular component

Movement is smoothed by _TURN_RATE, with speeds per mode.



It also clamps:

within scene bounds (with margins),

and within a “home radius” so they don’t wander too far from where they spawned.

enemy_ground

Hit checks

check_hits(frame):

advances the emplacements (using plane position from RUNTIME.flight if no explicit target provided)

checks for projectile hits (bullet/rocket/bomb) via segment-distance logic

if hit:

marks destroyed

spawns explosion

records impact with target=f"aaa_{idx}"

hides the Poly3DCollection

Render update

update(frame, tgt_x, tgt_y):

advances movement

computes turret angle to face aircraft

only recomputes rotation if the angle changed more than _ANGLE_EPS_DEG (1 degree) — nice micro-optimization

constructs world_faces by combining base + turret faces and offsetting by the emplacement center

writes verts into the Poly3DCollection

Targeting helpers

get_targets(frame) returns live centers (and advances simulation)

get_targets_with_ids(frame) returns (idx, center) pairs

get_home_targets_with_ids() returns home positions without advancing

get_anchor() returns a representative “anchor point” (average home xy)

has_live_targets() tells you if any are still alive

So this module already exposes “aim-assist style” hooks.

enemy_ground

Flight plan generation: flight_paths.py

This produces the aircraft’s “scripted” motion and the phase segmentation metadata.

flight_paths

The output

build_flight_plan(...) returns:

flight_x, flight_y, flight_z arrays (float64)

slice_map: Dict[str, Tuple[int,int]] mapping phase name → (start_index, end_index)

Phases include the canonical five plus:

Victory1

Victory2

Path composition

Each phase is generated as a segment between two 3D points with generate_path(...) (linear interpolation) plus optional curve “shaping”:

strafe_dive: makes Z drop using sine

escape_climb: adds a sinusoidal Z wobble

dogfight_maneuver: adds sinusoidal X/Y/Z oscillations

There’s a lot of care around:

bounding to terrain extents from _cfg (TERRAIN_XMIN/XMAX/YMIN/YMAX/ZMIN/ZMAX)

choosing start edges and opposite edges to create in-and-out arcs

variants like "high_alt", "low_alt", "north_arc", etc.

adding slight random “swing” in segments so repeated runs don’t look identical when RNG is enabled

So this is a “cinematic flight-plan generator” more than a physics flight model.

flight_paths

Scenario / decision logic: scenario.py

This file is pure logic—no rendering, no physics—just “when do we do actions.”

scenario

Precomputed schedule approach

build_action_schedule(slice_map, rng, ...) produces an ActionSchedule:

bullet_windows: list of BulletWindow(start,end,every,offset)

allows(frame) decides if bullets fire on that frame

rocket_frames: list of exact frames to launch rockets

bomb_frame: one frame (or None)

bogie_appear_frame, bogie_hit_frame, bogie_closing_factor

plus seed

This uses probabilities and ranges from ScenarioConfig:

whether to have strafe/dogfight/bombing actions at all

how many windows to create

bullet cadence per window

how many rockets and where

how close the bogie follows, and when it appears

This is basically a “script generator” that turns your phase slices into a coherent action story.

scenario

Dynamic decision approach

DecisionDirector is a stateful controller that:

constructs a per-frame phase_table from slice_map

maintains ammo counts and cooldowns

every decision_interval frames picks among:

hold

start a burst

launch rocket

drop bomb
using weighted random choice

Bursts continue across frames with their own internal cadence (burst_every) until duration ends or phase changes.



So you’ve got both:

deterministic-ish “schedule playback,” and

emergent-ish “AI decision loop”
available as interchangeable orchestration styles.

scenario

Weather: weather.py

A clean little deterministic generator:

WeatherDirector.build(seed=...) picks:

wind speed + direction → wind_x, wind_y

a vertical wind component wind_z

gust as a factor of wind

turbulence scalar

visibility_km

Returns WeatherState(seed, wind, gust, turbulence, visibility_km).



This likely feeds into RUNTIME.environment (though the glue isn’t in these files).

ai.py (legacy stub)

This is intentionally empty and exists to keep old imports from exploding:

“AI behavior lives in enemy_bogies and enemy_ground.”

ai

Recurring patterns I’m tracking (these become obvious “library seams” later)

No coding yet—just calling out the shapes that repeat:

Segment-to-point hit testing
The same math pattern exists in:

aircraft hit checks,

bogie hit checks,

ground emplacement hit checks.

Impact recording format
Multiple modules append similarly structured dicts into RUNTIME.impacts.

Global module-level runtime state
Aircraft rendering, bogie, ground emplacements all store state in module globals and expose init/reset/update style functions.

Determinism controls

scenario uses seeds and reproducible RNG,

ground system can be seeded (configure(seed)),

weather uses seeds.

Typed vs runtime dtype choices

flight paths are float64,

projectile paths are float32,

mesh work arrays are float32,

bogie timeline arrays are float64.
Nothing “wrong” here—just something a future library needs to standardize or at least document.

Subtle “gotchas” worth remembering

These are not criticisms—just “landmines” you’ll want me to remember when we start modularizing:

Bomb hits on the player are disabled unless env var says otherwise (WARBITS_AIRCRAFT_BOMB_HITS).

aircraft_hits

Aircraft rendering requires calling register_axes(ax) before step_aircraft(...) will do anything.

aircraft

Ground emplacements advance movement in multiple public calls (update, check_hits, get_targets…), but they protect against double-advancing with last_frame == frame. This is intentional but important when wiring the main loop.

enemy_ground

Bogie is_alive() is “not destroyed” rather than “currently visible/appeared,” because pre-appearance frames are NaN but still considered “alive.”

enemy_bogies

Thought for 14m 4s

According to the project files you uploaded on January 3, 2026, this batch is basically your “how to run it + how it looks + what exists in the world” layer: a CLI entrypoint, global settings/styling, and the big JSON spec vaults (vehicles/weapons/warheads/sensors/terrain).



Below is what each of these ten files is doing, and how they fit into the application.

1) warbits_cli.py — the command-line “front door”

This file is a thin CLI wrapper around the actual simulation/animation runner.

What it does

Builds an argparse CLI with flags like:

--loop to restart the simulation after it ends (intended for demo/continuous run behavior)

--max-perf to force a performance mode

--dump-config to print out the effective settings/config instead of running the sim
These are all wired by setting environment variables and/or dispatching to a runner.

Applies “performance mode” behavior:

If --max-perf is set, it sets env vars (notably WARBITS_MAX_PERF=1) and also calls a helper to “use all cores”.

Calls the animation/simulation runner:

It imports and calls run_animation() from warbits.scene.animation. (That module isn’t in the files you’ve uploaded yet, but this makes it clear where execution ultimately goes.)

Why it matters architecturally

This file is “policy & wiring,” not core logic:

It doesn’t simulate anything itself.

It chooses config overrides, then hands off to the actual visual sim engine.

2) settings.py — the “everything knob” for sim + rendering

This is a central configuration module that defines a lot of runtime behavior: rendering scale, performance toggles, terrain bounds, physics-ish constants, etc.

Big themes inside settings.py
A) Project identity + defaults

Defines metadata and a default vehicle selection.

B) Environment-driven configuration

Provides helper functions to read env vars as bool/int/float/str with defaults (so you can do WARBITS_FPS=... or similar).

Uses env flags for things like auto quality/perf mode behavior (more on that below).

C) Performance/quality scaling

There’s a clear intent: the same sim can run as a pretty visualization or as a “fast loop”.

Settings include things like FPS targets, frame skipping, and a “perf mode.”

D) World bounds: terrain + scene box

This module establishes global coordinate limits (terrain extents and scene extents).
This is important because almost every other system (aircraft motion, projectile motion, camera framing, terrain sampling) needs shared world bounds to stay consistent.

E) Figure/canvas creation for rendering

There’s a helper that constructs the visualization canvas (Matplotlib 3D axes), applies your house style, and configures the 3D view:

create_scene_canvas(...) builds a Figure + Axes3D, applies style helpers, and sets axis bounds and view parameters.

This connects directly to style.py (below), which holds the reusable styling functions.

Why it matters architecturally

This file is the global constants & configuration hub.
When you later build “libraries,” this will likely become either:

a “settings package” (typed settings objects + validators), or

split into render_settings, physics_settings, world_settings, etc.

But right now: it’s the authoritative global knob-board.

3) style.py — reusable Matplotlib styling utilities

This module is strictly about presentation.

What it contains

apply_style() sets Matplotlib rcParams for a consistent look (dark theme, grid/lines/font tweaks, etc.).

configure_3d_axes(ax, ...) standardizes the 3D axes: limits, aspect, viewpoint, and overall readability.

make_fullscreen(fig) tries multiple backend-specific strategies to fullscreen/maximize the figure window.

Why it matters architecturally

This is a clean “leaf module”:

It shouldn’t depend on sim logic.

It’s safe to reuse anywhere you create plots/figures.

And settings.py is already calling into it for the main scene canvas.

4) sensors.json — sensor capability dataset (targeting pods / sights / etc.)

This is a structured dataset that looks like it came from a War Thunder data extraction / spreadsheet pipeline (based on the sources field).

Structure (typical fields)

Entries include things like:

id, name

platform_name (what platform the sensor is associated with)

role (ex: targeting pod vs built-in)

sensor_type (ex: thermal, TV, etc.)

Resolution fields, zoom ranges, and other constraints

sources referencing a workbook/sheet for traceability

sensors

Why it matters architecturally

This is “ground truth” data for a future sensor/EO/IR/radar modeling layer.
In the Python files you’ve uploaded so far, I don’t yet see code that loads or uses this dataset directly—so either that loader lives in files you haven’t sent yet, or it’s planned for the library work phase.

5) terrain.json — surface types + ground interaction parameters

This is a small dataset listing terrain surface categories.

Structure

Each entry includes:

surface name

biome

friction_coefficient

roughness

optional notes

Why it matters

This looks like the start of a “ground physics / mobility / traction” layer:

Ground vehicles could use friction + roughness.

Aircraft ground roll / runway vs grass behavior could use it too.

6) vehicle_specs.py — legacy placeholder

This file is explicitly a stub:

It exports VEHICLE_SPECS = {} and says it exists for “legacy imports” and that the data now lives in vehicles.json.

So: do not treat this as authoritative data—it’s compatibility scaffolding.

7) vehicles.json — aircraft performance dataset

This is the real vehicle spec vault (currently aircraft only, based on vehicle_type).

Structure (typical fields)

Entries include:

id, name, vehicle_type

max_speed_mps and max_speed_altitude_m

fuel_full_duration_min

radiator flags like variable_radiator / variable_oil_radiator

best climb metrics:

best_climb_altitude_m

best_climb_rate_mps

a detailed climb_profile array: altitude steps with speed and climb times (nominal vs WEP)

vehicles

Also includes sources that reference WarThunder FactChecker workbook/sheets for traceability.

vehicles

Why it matters architecturally

This dataset is rich enough to support:

climb/energy modeling

performance-limited AI behaviors (choose climb to optimal altitude, etc.)

scenario generation constraints (e.g., “spawn aircraft at altitude where they can actually sustain speed”).

8) warheads.json — warhead properties (explosive mass, penetration, fusing)

This is a separate dataset of warheads, keyed by a warhead id, and (importantly) each warhead also references the weapon it belongs to.

Structure (typical fields)

Warhead entries include:

id

weapon_id (so you can map warhead → weapon)

explosive/penetration fields:

explosive_mass_kg

penetration_mm (when applicable)

fuse behavior:

proximity fuse booleans and parameters (proximity_fuse_*)

impact fuse delay/sensitivity (impact_fuse_delay_m, impact_fuse_sensitivity_mm)

warheads

warheads

Plus warhead_type (“HE”, “HEAT”, “Tandem HEAT”, etc.) and sources references.

warheads

Why it matters architecturally

This is a clean separation of concerns:

Weapons define flight/propulsion/guidance.

Warheads define terminal effect + fusing.

That split is going to pay off once you build a proper damage/effects library.

9) weapon_specs.py — legacy placeholder

Same pattern as vehicle_specs.py:

Exports empty WEAPON_SPECS = {}

States it exists for legacy imports, and the real data is in weapons.json.

10) weapons.json — the main weapon spec vault

This is the big one. It’s a large list of weapon entries, and the schema clearly varies by weapon category.

Common pattern

Weapons include:

id, name

weapon_type (example: air-to-air missiles show up as "air_to_air_missile")

a sources field referencing the extraction workbook and sheet.

Missiles (example characteristics)

For missile-like weapons, you see fields such as:

geometry / drag / mass (diameter_m, length_m, drag_coefficient, mass_initial_kg, etc.)

propulsion (“booster” thrust/time, burn sequencing)

guidance tags (IR / SARH / ARH / etc.)

and crucially: a warhead_id linking to warheads.json

Bombs / guided bombs (example characteristics)

Bomb-ish entries have their own fields (still with mass/drag-like terms), plus guidance-related fields when they’re guided, and still tie back to a warhead via warhead_id.

A very important “data-shape” observation

A lot of the deeper parameters are packed into an attributes object with extremely verbose keys (they look like spreadsheet column headers turned into JSON keys).



That’s not “bad,” but it’s a strong hint that a future library will want:

a normalization layer (map verbose keys → stable internal field names)

type coercion + validation

schema per weapon type (missile vs bomb vs rocket)

How this batch connects to the rest of the code you sent earlier

warbits_cli.py chooses runtime flags and hands off to a scene/animation driver.

settings.py defines world bounds and creates the 3D scene canvas that other simulation/render modules will draw into.

style.py centralizes the Matplotlib presentation rules used by that canvas.

vehicles.json, weapons.json, warheads.json, sensors.json, terrain.json are the current “facts about the world.” The *_specs.py modules are explicitly legacy stubs.

Got it. I’ve pulled these into a single mental model (no building/refactoring yet—just understanding what you already have), and the picture is getting pretty clear.

What this application is “doing” at a high level (from the files so far)

This is a 3D sortie / gunnery / battlefield micro-sim that looks designed to run as a Matplotlib animation (Axes3D), with:

A precomputed flight path (the “sortie” broken into phases like Approach/Strafe/Bombing/Escape/Dogfight)

A global runtime state that stores:

the aircraft’s current position/velocity,

active projectile trajectories (bullets/rockets/bombs),

active VFX (explosions, parachutes),

a simple “environment” (wind, turbulence, visibility)

A set of scene-integrated physics modules for bullets/rockets/bombs that:

precompute trajectories,

advance the “sample index” each frame,

draw/update a scatter marker,

remove projectiles when they hit terrain,

optionally spawn explosions and log impacts

Two enemy systems:

Enemy bogie (air target): appears late, chases, can get hit, tumbles, deploys parachute, hits ground

Enemy ground AAA (emplacements): mobile/patrolling units with turret tracking, can be destroyed by projectiles

A lot of the “simulation engine” is already modular in spirit: you have a clean split between pure physics kernels (“simulate X trajectory”) and scene/animation façades (“schedule a rocket launch, update markers, spawn explosion, record impact”).

The central nervous system: state.py

Everything orbits around a single global runtime object: RUNTIME.

state



Key idea: projectiles are stored as contiguous NumPy buffers, not as Python objects per projectile. That’s a serious performance-oriented design choice.

ProjectileBuffer is a struct-of-arrays store:

_paths: shape (capacity, 3, max_samples) float32

_lengths: number of samples for each trajectory

_sample_index: “where am I” along that trajectory this frame

ring-buffer behavior (_cursor) to overwrite oldest slots

fast “active rows” list so you only update what matters

RuntimeState holds:

active_bullets, active_rockets, active_bombs (each a ProjectileBuffer)

explosions, parachutes, impacts (Python lists of state dicts)

flight (frame, plane_pos, plane_vel)

environment (wind/gust/turbulence/visibility)

This is the “truth store” that almost all subsystems read/write.

Flight path + phases: flight_paths.py (+ phases.py)

The sortie is built as a stitched path with named phases and a slice-map.

flight_paths

DEFAULT_PHASES defines phase durations (Approach, Strafe, Bombing, Escape, Dogfight)

build_flight_plan(...) returns:

flight_x, flight_y, flight_z arrays

slice_map: {phase_name: (start_frame, end_frame)}

It also supports “variant” planning (different entry edges, arcs, altitude biases, etc.), and makes sure the flight stays inside terrain bounds (read from settings).



phases.py is basically a compatibility wrapper that re-exports the default phase table. (It’s a “don’t break old imports” file.)

Scenario timing and “decisions”: scenario.py

This is your “mission director” logic.

scenario



There are two related but distinct ideas in this file:

1) Deterministic schedule building (ScenarioDirector / ActionSchedule)

Given the slice_map of phases, it generates:

bullet_windows: time windows during Strafe/Dogfight where bullets are allowed periodically

rocket_frames: explicit frames to launch rockets

bomb_frame: a single drop frame (optional)

bogie-related events:

bogie_appear_frame

bogie_hit_frame

bogie_closing_factor

a seed for reproducibility

This looks like it’s meant for “scripted-but-random” runs.

2) Per-frame weighted decision making (DecisionDirector)

This is more dynamic: every decision_interval frames it chooses between:

hold

start/continue a bullet burst

launch rocket

drop bomb

It tracks ammo/cooldowns and respects the current phase (Strafe/Dogfight/Bombing constraints).



So you already have both “preplanned” and “reactive AI-like” options.

Entities and visuals: aircraft + enemy bogie + ground AAA
aircraft.py: mesh creation + fast updating + glow pulse

This provides:

a tiny “plane wedge” mesh generator (player aircraft and bogie)

optimized updating by caching base faces and applying a fast transform

runtime helpers to register an axis, reset, and step the player aircraft each frame (including the pulsing glow effect)

This is very Matplotlib-3D specific: it’s managing Poly3DCollection, cached verts, and some compatibility shims around set_verts/get_verts.

aircraft

enemy_bogies.py: bogie pathing + hit logic + parachute + crash

This module is a self-contained subsystem:

Precomputes bogie path arrays (_bog_x/_bog_y/_bog_z) that “close” toward the player’s path starting at appear_at

Keeps terrain clearance by using sample_height(...)

Hit detection:

checks segments of bullets/rockets/bombs vs bogie position (closest point on last segment) so high-speed projectiles don’t “tunnel”

can be forced with a deterministic hit_frame override

On hit:

triggers an explosion

records an impact event

transitions to a tumbling/falling motion

spawns a parachute once

detonates on ground contact / time limit and removes mesh

This is one of the best “complete stories” in the codebase so far: spawn → chase → get hit → bail-out → crash.

enemy_bogies

enemy_ground.py: AAA emplacements that move + track + can die

This is a surprisingly rich little AI:

Emplacements have:

a base + turret box mesh

a home point

patrol targets and an orbiting patrol behavior

mode switching based on distance to the aircraft:

patrol → engage → evade (and back) using distance thresholds

They move every frame via _advance(...), clamped inside terrain bounds

The turret rotates (in Z) to track the plane XY

Projectile hit checks use the same “segment distance” approach as bogie/aircraft hits

When destroyed:

explosion

impact record

hides the corresponding Poly3DCollection

Also note: it provides targeting helpers (get_targets_with_ids, get_anchor, has_live_targets) that scream “future aim-assist / mission logic hooks.”

enemy_ground

Weapons & physics modules (and the VFX that make it feel alive)
Ballistics: ballistics.py

Two layers:

Physics kernel: simulate_bullet_trajectory(...)

supports single vector or batch (N,3)

uses gravity, optional drag, and wind (defaults to RUNTIME.environment.wind)

has a “fast path” if drag=0 and wind=0

Scene helpers:

spawn(...) creates a burst, registers trajectories into RUNTIME.active_bullets

update(...) advances bullets, updates a shared scatter marker, removes bullets that hit terrain

This module is optimized for lots of bullets: spread is precomputed into a table and reused so you don’t call RNG constantly.



ballistics_fast.py is another compatibility wrapper (re-export layer).

Rockets: rockets.py

Again, two layers:

simulate_rocket_trajectory(...): thrust phase then coast; optional drag; wind from environment; has a “cheap path” if drag/wind/mass_flow are 0

Scene façade:

schedule_launch(frame)

step(frame, plane_pos, plane_vel, ax)

maintains a sorted queue of scheduled launches

impacts with terrain spawn explosions and record impact events

Bombs: bombs.py

Same pattern:

simulate_bomb_trajectory(...) (gravity + drag + wind)

schedule_release(frame)

step(frame, plane_pos, plane_vel, ax)

impacts spawn explosions and record impact events

maintains an internal scatter artist for bombs

Explosions: explosions.py

Object-pooled explosion meshes (sphere-ish Poly3DCollection) that:

expand and fade over _EXP_LIMIT frames

can be styled (sphere vs mushroom)

must be driven by a per-frame update_explosion() call

Parachute: parachute.py

Also object-pooled, with a multi-stage deployment feel:

pilot box + canopy + cords + plume

optional “physics mode” with drag and wind

per-frame updater update_parachute()

So explosions and parachutes are not just “sprites”; they’re actual 3D geometry being updated, which is why you see pooling and caching everywhere (Matplotlib 3D can get slow fast).

Hit detection against the player aircraft: aircraft_hits.py

This file handles incoming rocket/bomb hits against the player craft:

Uses segment-distance checks on rockets and bombs

Has minimum sample thresholds so you don’t “hit yourself” immediately after spawn

Bomb hits are toggleable via env var (WARBITS_AIRCRAFT_BOMB_HITS)

On hit it:

removes the projectile row from the buffer

spawns explosion

records an impact event

aircraft_hits

Weather: weather.py

WeatherDirector builds a WeatherState from a seed:

wind vector (x/y direction + vertical component)

gust as a fraction of wind

turbulence scalar

visibility range

This doesn’t “apply itself”; it’s meant to be consumed by whatever scene/animation module sets RUNTIME.environment.

weather

supports a --max-perf mode that tries to enable “use all cores” via a utility module

So: the orchestration is almost certainly in warbits/scene/animation.py, which you haven’t sent yet.

The implied per-frame loop (inferred from how modules are written)

Without seeing warbits.scene.animation yet, the modules strongly suggest a loop like:

Update RUNTIME.flight (frame index, plane_pos, plane_vel) from the flight path arrays

Draw/update the player aircraft mesh (aircraft.step_aircraft(...))

Enemy updates:

bogie update (enemy_bogies.update(frame))

AAA update + hit checks (enemy_ground.check_hits(frame) and/or enemy_ground.update(...))

Weapon events (from schedule/decisions):

if bullets: ballistics.spawn(...)

if rocket: rockets.schedule_launch(frame) then rockets.step(...)

if bomb: bombs.schedule_release(frame) then bombs.step(...)

Projectile visuals update:

ballistics.update(frame, ax)

rockets.step(...) (already both advances + draws)

bombs.step(...) (already both advances + draws)

VFX update:

explosions.update_explosion()

parachute.update_parachute()

Optional: aircraft hit checks (aircraft_hits.check_aircraft_hits(frame, plane_pos))

That’s the “heartbeat” the code is begging to run under.

Why ProjectileBuffer matters

ProjectileBuffer is a struct-of-arrays, NumPy-backed ring-ish system that can hold up to thousands of trajectories, where each projectile is stored as a (3, T) path and a sample index that advances each frame. That’s how you can animate “lots of bullets” without Python objects per bullet.

state



This buffer design is one of the main architectural anchor points for later “library building” because it’s the shared contract between:

physics solvers (generate x/y/z arrays),

render updaters (sample current positions),

hit detection (segment checks between last and current sample).

Got it — I’ve ingested this batch and built a working mental model of how these pieces hang together right now, plus what they’re clearly setting you up to do later (data-driven weapons/vehicles/sensors).



Below is my “I can navigate this codebase blindfolded” understanding of these files — no coding, no refactors, just an accurate map of what exists and how it behaves.

What this application is (from these files)

This is Warbits: a Python + NumPy + Matplotlib 3D animation “flight & gunnery sim” where:

The player aircraft follows a precomputed flight plan (arrays of X/Y/Z positions).

The sim spawns projectiles (bullets, rockets, bombs) that follow precomputed trajectories (also stored as sampled arrays).

You have enemy actors:

an air bogie (enemy aircraft) that appears late and closes on the player,

and ground AAA emplacements that track the player (and also move with simple AI).

Hits create explosions and are recorded as structured impact events.

There’s an (optional) parachute sequence when the bogie gets hit.

It’s heavily optimized around:

NumPy arrays + precomputed paths,

and Matplotlib artist reuse (update-in-place instead of recreate).

All of this is orchestrated by modules you haven’t provided yet (notably warbits/scene/animation.py), but the behavior and interfaces are already very visible from what we have.

The core “runtime spine”: logic/state.py
RUNTIME (global singleton)

state.py defines the global runtime container used everywhere:

RUNTIME.flight: live aircraft position/velocity (plane_pos, plane_vel, frame).

RUNTIME.environment: wind/gust/turbulence/visibility (wind is already used by ballistics/rockets/bombs/parachute).

RUNTIME.active_bullets, active_rockets, active_bombs: each is a ProjectileBuffer.

RUNTIME.explosions, RUNTIME.parachutes: lists (though explosions/parachutes also manage their own pools/active lists).

RUNTIME.impacts: list of dict events — the “combat log”.

ProjectileBuffer design (important for everything else)

This is a struct-of-arrays (SoA) trajectory buffer:

Stores trajectories as paths[projectile, axis(3), sample] in float32.

Tracks per-projectile:

lengths (how many samples in the stored trajectory),

sample_index (which sample is currently “active”),

_active_rows and _active_pos for dense iteration (only active projectiles).

Supports:

.add() trajectory batches (ring-buffer overwrite of oldest if needed),

.step() to advance all active sample indices,

.remove() and .clear(),

.sample_positions() which returns current (xs, ys, zs, rows) for all active projectiles.

This choice is why hit-detection is done via sampled segments (not continuous integration every frame): your projectiles are basically “playback of precomputed tracks”.

The physics layer: bullets, rockets, bombs, terrain, explosions, parachute
physics/terrain.py

This is procedural terrain generation + fast height sampling:

generate_terrain(...) makes a grid using sin/cos patterns + noise, with multiple named TerrainProfiles (rolling, desert, mountain, forest, urban).

draw_terrain(ax, ...) calls plot_surface and also:

caches the grid via set_active_terrain(...)

stabilizes color range per (profile, seed) to reduce visual “colormap flicker”.

sample_height(x,y) uses bilinear interpolation on the cached grid.

Many other modules call sample_height for:

projectile ground collision,

keeping bogies above terrain,

grounding AAA emplacements,

ensuring explosions spawn at the terrain surface.

physics/ballistics.py

Two roles here:

Physics kernel: simulate_bullet_trajectory(...)

Vectorized solver: can take (3,) or (N,3) for pos/vel.

Uses:

gravity,

optional wind (defaults to RUNTIME.environment.wind),

quadratic-ish drag (it applies v -= drag * rel * speed * dt).

“Fast path” for drag=0 and no wind uses closed-form / cumsum-ish calculations.

Scene integration helpers: reset, spawn, update

spawn(...) generates a burst and adds it into RUNTIME.active_bullets.

update(...):

fetches current bullet sample positions,

checks them against terrain height,

removes impacted bullets,

keeps a single shared Matplotlib scatter artist updated in-place,

then calls RUNTIME.active_bullets.step().

You also have a spread table + caching to make bursts look slightly imperfect without allocating constantly.

physics/rockets.py

Similarly split:

Physics kernel: simulate_rocket_trajectory(...)

Forward-fired rocket:

initial direction is from plane velocity (defaults to forward if speed ~0),

constant thrust for thrust_dur,

optional mass-flow model (mass decreases → acceleration scales),

wind + drag + gravity.

Scene façade:

schedule_launch(frame_idx) stores a sorted list of launch frames.

step(frame, plane_pos, plane_vel, ax):

spawns rockets whose scheduled frame equals current frame,

updates scatter marker in-place,

checks terrain impacts (using sample_height),

spawns explosions and appends impact events.

physics/bombs.py

Bombs are “scheduled release” rather than queued list:

schedule_release(frame_idx) sets a single _release_at.

step(...):

when frame matches _release_at, it generates a bomb trajectory and adds to RUNTIME.active_bombs.

checks terrain collisions each frame:

if impact: spawns a mushroom explosion, logs impact event, removes projectile.

updates a scatter marker and blinks color based on altitude.

There’s explicit attention to time-step consistency:

it derives a scale using SIM_DT_MS / BOMB_DT to keep the initial velocity aligned with the sim’s frame step vs integration dt.

physics/explosions.py

Explosion VFX is self-contained and pooled:

You call register_axes(ax) once.

spawn_explosion((x,y,z), scale=..., style=...) grabs pooled object or creates one.

Each explosion is a Poly3DCollection sphere mesh that:

grows over _EXP_LIMIT frames,

fades alpha over time,

supports "sphere" or "mushroom" style shaping.

physics/parachute.py

This is a full ejection+chute sequence with pooling:

register_axes(ax) sets the axes and cleans old artists if axes changes.

_Parachute stages:

rocket-seat boost (plume visible),

short freefall (no canopy),

inflation stage (radius grows),

glide to ground.

Two modes:

“simple” mode: fixed per-frame drop and decorative sway.

“physics” mode (gated by _cfg.PARACHUTE_PHYSICS):

integrates velocity with drag + gravity relative to wind (RUNTIME.environment.wind).

It renders:

canopy hemisphere mesh,

pilot block,

cords as a Line3DCollection,

plume as a small triangle/quad-like poly.

The code is clearly written to minimize allocations (cached arrays for verts/segments).

The “actors”: player aircraft, enemy bogie, enemy AAA, and hit detection
logic/aircraft.py

This is the player aircraft model + pulsing glow:

Defines a simple “wedge-ish” aircraft mesh (faces).

Uses Poly3DCollection for the mesh and a scatter marker for glow.

Keeps global cached artist handles:

register_axes(ax) stores the Axes3D.

reset_aircraft() removes old.

step_aircraft(pos, vel, frame) updates verts in-place and applies a pulse that oscillates between green ↔ white-ish glow.

Performance-wise: it avoids re-allocating faces; it updates an existing vertex array and reuses the same collection.

logic/enemy_bogies.py

Enemy aircraft logic is deliberately cheap:

init(ax, flight_x, flight_y, flight_z, slice_map) stores references to the player path arrays.

Bogie path is created as arrays _bog_x/_bog_y/_bog_z:

it “appears” near the end of Escape or near end of flight by default,

spawns off-screen-ish and then closes toward the player with a closing_factor,

maintains a separation offset and terrain clearance via sample_height.

Hit detection:

Uses segment-based closest-point distance against projectile segments using the buffer’s sample_index:

rockets and bullets count,

bombs are excluded (makes sense given current gameplay).

If hit:

spawns explosion at hit point,

logs an impact event (target="bogie"),

enters post-hit tumble: drifting spiral + falling under gravity,

deploys parachute once,

explodes when hitting terrain.

There’s also a deterministic hit option via configure(hit_frame=...).

logic/enemy_ground.py

Ground targets are AAA emplacements with both:

turret tracking (rotates to face player),

and movement AI (patrol/engage/evade).

Structure:

Two emplacements by default (two Poly3DCollections).

Each emplacement is a dataclass storing:

base/turret faces,

cached world faces array,

position/home/patrol targets,

velocity and behavior mode.

Movement:

Uses distance bands to switch modes:

patrol: pick patrol target, orbit around it, timer-based retargeting,

engage: orbit around player at engage radius,

evade: move away from player with some lateral component.

Uses smoothing for turning (_TURN_RATE) and clamps within scene bounds + within a “home radius”.

Hits:

Uses the same segment-based hit logic against bullets/rockets/bombs (different radii per weapon type).

On hit:

spawns explosion,

logs impact (target="aaa_{idx}"),

hides its Poly3DCollection.

It also exposes:

get_targets(...) and get_targets_with_ids(...) for aim assist / targeting.

get_anchor() (average home spawn center) useful for flight-path targeting.

logic/aircraft_hits.py

This is hit detection against the player aircraft:

Checks rocket segments (and optionally bomb segments) near the aircraft position.

If impact:

removes projectile from active buffer,

spawns a small explosion,

logs impact event (target="aircraft").

This is purely “effects + logging” — it does not destroy the aircraft.

The “behavior directors”: scenario.py and weather.py
logic/scenario.py

Two separate mechanisms exist:

Precomputed schedule (ActionSchedule)

Based on the flight plan’s slice_map (Approach/Strafe/Bombing/Escape/Dogfight).

Builds:

bullet windows (start/end/every/offset),

rocket frames (list),

bomb frame (single),

bogie appear/hit frames (optional),

bogie closing factor,

seed.

Dynamic decision engine (DecisionDirector)

Uses a periodic decision interval and weighted random choice:

hold,

burst (bullets),

rocket,

bomb.

Enforces ammo and cooldown windows.

Restricts choices by phase (Strafe/Dogfight/Bombing).

So you can run the sim as:

“scripted per-loop schedule”, or

“AI decision-making each interval”.

logic/weather.py

Simple per-loop weather generator:

Uses a seed to generate:

wind vector (speed + direction + vertical component),

gust vector (scaled wind),

turbulence scalar,

visibility.

This is already compatible with:

RUNTIME.environment.wind usage in the physics solvers and parachute physics.

Flight plan generation: logic/flight_paths.py (+ phases.py)

flight_paths.py builds the player’s path and exposes:

DEFAULT_PHASES: counts + colors for phases in canonical order.

build_flight_plan(...):

chooses start edge and opposite edge based on variant/target anchor/start_pos,

generates 5 legs (Approach, Strafe, Bombing, Escape, Dogfight),

adds “Victory1” and “Victory2” fly-by loops,

returns arrays flight_x, flight_y, flight_z and a slice_map dict mapping phase name to index ranges.

It clamps all points inside scene bounds (with margins), and can inject randomized mid-turn “swings” to avoid overly straight lines.



phases.py is just a compatibility re-export of DEFAULT_PHASES.

UI + config: settings.py, style.py, warbits_cli.py, wrappers
config/settings.py

This file is the “configuration mother ship.”

Reads lots of WARBITS_* env vars to drive:

sim dt,

terrain bounds,

drag coefficients,

rendering/perf mode,

camera behavior,

figure sizing and canvas pixel budgeting,

scatter depthshade toggles,

parachute physics toggles, etc.

Does screen-size detection (tkinter) and attempts to scale canvas.

Contains perf mode logic like pixel caps.

config/style.py

Matplotlib styling helpers:

dark theme,

axes configuration (limits/view/aspect),

fullscreen helper.

CLI: warbits_cli.py

Subcommands:

warbits run (default),

warbits config (dumps resolved settings).

Has backend guard (rejects Agg/SVG in non-interactive environment).

Optional “max perf” warmup calls concurrency.use_all_cores().

Compatibility wrappers

These exist to keep old imports working while the package layout evolves:

ai.py (placeholder; real logic now in enemy modules)

models.py (reexports aircraft model builders)

effects.py (reexports explosion API)

mpl_setup.py (reexports style API)

hardware.py (reexports detect_hardware)

vehicle_specs.py and weapon_specs.py (placeholders, likely replaced by JSON-driven data later)

Data assets: the JSON files

These look like your future canonical data layer (even if not fully wired into the sim yet).

Quick inventory:

…and loadouts currently empty.

Small “realism knobs” dataset:

IDs align with terrain profile aliasing (desert_sand, urban_asphalt, etc.)

A list of sensor definitions:

role (targeting pod / sight / etc),

and sources.

A list of vehicle performance definitions (aircraft-heavy from the sample):

weapons.json + warheads.json

Weapons are detailed and schema-heavy:

weapons.json includes:

guidance type, ranges, booster thrust/time, seeker properties, etc,

plus a huge attributes bag of extra/irregular values.

explosive mass, penetration, fuse sensitivity/delay, proximity fuse info.

Linkage:

loadouts.json

Explicitly stubbed (“irregular schema; defer parsing”). That matches the warning in data_summary.json.

The per-frame “game loop” as implied by these modules

Even without seeing scene/animation.py, the loop basically has to look like:

Update RUNTIME.flight.frame, plane_pos, plane_vel from the flight plan arrays.

Render/update the player aircraft mesh (aircraft.step_aircraft).

Spawn projectiles based on scenario/decision logic (scenario.py) and feed them into:

bullets, rockets, bombs (either via engagement.py or the per-weapon scene façades).

Move/update enemies:

enemy_ground.update(frame, plane_x, plane_y)

enemy_bogies.update(frame)

Step projectiles + draw markers:

ballistics.update(...), rockets.step(...), bombs.step(...) (depending on which pathway is used in your animation module).

Hit checks:

aircraft hit checks (aircraft_hits.check_hits(frame, aircraft_pos)),

ground hit checks (enemy_ground.check_hits(frame)),

bogie hit checks are inside bogie update.

Update VFX:

update_explosion()

update_parachute()

Loop/reset:

reset terrain + enemies + runtime buffers when the sortie ends, depending on loop settings.

Patterns that scream “future library boundaries” (no coding yet, just map)

These are the natural seams your code already implies:

State library

ProjectileBuffer, RuntimeState, typed impact events.

Physics library

ballistics kernels (bullet/rocket/bomb),

terrain sampling,

weather/wind effects,

parachute dynamics.

Collision / hit detection library

the segment-distance hit kernel appears in three places (bogies, ground, aircraft hits).

this will want to become a shared “geometry/collision” module.

Rendering / artist management library

aircraft mesh updates,

pooled explosions,

pooled parachutes,

scatter markers for projectiles.

Scenario + decision library

slice-map aware schedule builder,

decision director with ammo/cooldowns.

Data model + ingestion library

JSON schemas for weapons/warheads/vehicles/sensors/terrain,

cross-link resolution (weapon ↔ warhead, loadouts ↔ platforms, etc).

Known/explicit issues already tracked (from TRACKER.md + what I see in code)

A few that are already documented in your tracker and match the code patterns:

“argmax t=0 hit bug” in fast solver branches (bullet/rocket): if the first sample is already “hit”, argmax returns 0 which is ambiguous and currently treated as “no hit” in those fast branches.

Solvers swallow exceptions silently (they return empty arrays), which is good for not crashing a demo but bad for debugging.

ProjectileBuffer max_samples hard cap can be exceeded if dt is too small and max_time too large.

Parachute sway freeze after stage 2 is called out in tracker; the stage tick/reset logic is where that would happen.

How simulation “moves” right now (high-level mechanics)

There’s a global runtime state (RUNTIME) that stores “active” projectiles and impacts, and those projectiles live in a ProjectileBuffer optimized for animation (arrays of precomputed points + a stepping cursor). This is one of the core performance design choices.

flight_paths

flight_paths

You have two scenario control styles:

ActionSchedule: precomputed random-ish events by frame

DecisionDirector: dynamic decisions per frame (bullets/rockets/bombs), wired to “spawn” functions.

Spawning weapons is centralized through functions like spawn_burst, spawn_rocket, spawn_bomb, which call the physics solvers and then register the resulting trajectories into RUNTIME.

Your physics solvers already include hooks for wind + terrain collision:

Ballistics imports RUNTIME and sample_height and is designed to clamp paths and stop at terrain.

ballistics
