Quick reality check on your downloaded model file types (for ingestion)

Since you said you don’t have Blender right now:



Best formats for our pipeline (lowest pain):

.obj ✅

.glb / glTF ✅

Potentially usable but typically needs extra tooling / optional deps:

.fbx ⚠️ (often needs Assimp/FBX SDK/convert step)

.usdc (USD) ⚠️ (usually requires Pixar USD Python bindings)

Not usable without Blender or special parsers:

.blend ❌ (treat as “source asset,” convert to glb/obj elsewhere)

So when you’re downloading stuff to feed this system, prioritize OBJ or GLB first.

4) Mount weapons using anchors (runtime)

This is the baseline “missile under wing” behavior:

import numpy as np
from warbits.visual.registry import VisualRegistry
from warbits.visual.attach import Pose, AttachmentSpec, attach_child_pose

reg = VisualRegistry.from_files(
    "data/visual/blueprints.jsonl",
    anchors_jsonl_path="data/visual/anchors.jsonl",
)

parent_id = "aircraft:f16"
parent_pose = Pose(pos_m=np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1000.0]), rot=np.eye(3))
parent_scale = 1.0

anchors = reg.get_anchors(parent_id)

spec = AttachmentSpec(
    child_blueprint_id="weapon:aim9",
    parent_anchor="pylon_left_1",
    offset_local_m=np.array([0.0, 0.0, -0.15]),
)

child_pose = attach_child_pose(
    parent_pose=parent_pose,
    parent_scale=parent_scale,
    anchors=anchors,
    spec=spec,
)

# Render parent + child as separate instances (same renderer layer).

5) Scale-fit when you have real dimensions

Uniform scale (safe for accurate mesh blueprints):

from warbits.visual.scale_fit import TargetDims, compute_uniform_scale

V, E = reg.get_geometry("aircraft:f16", distance_m=1500.0)

scale = compute_uniform_scale(
    V,
    TargetDims(length_m=15.0, span_m=10.0),
)

Your 3D files: what to download / use / convert

From what you uploaded:

✅ Works with the current ingest stack (trimesh-based):

.glb / .gltf

.obj

❌ Not usable directly (needs conversion):

.fbx (trimesh typically won’t load FBX without extra toolchain)

.usdc (USD binary)

.blend (Blender-native)

So the rule is simple:
Download or export GLB/GLTF whenever possible. OBJ is the runner-up.



Also: if your GLB has mesh names like Cube.005, your generated blueprint IDs will be similarly ugly. It still works (you can alias it in mapping), but for sanity you’ll eventually want meaningful mesh names before export.

Free / open “Visual Blueprint DB” sources worth grabbing

Here are solid places to pull free models you can legally use as reference assets, and convert into your blueprints.jsonl via your ingest pipeline.

OpenVSP Airshow (massive aircraft model library)

OpenVSP’s team launched Airshow as the successor to the old Hangar, and states that all Hangar models were ported into it.
openvsp.org

This is extremely useful because VSP models can be exported (OBJ/STL/etc) and then turned into wireframe blueprints in your pipeline.

Smithsonian 3D (explicit Open Access examples)

Smithsonian has 3D objects marked Open access media: CC0 (public domain dedication). Example: the Wright Flyer 1903 scan.
3d.si.edu

Even if not “modern military,” it’s a clean, legally safe source of real scanned geometry for testing your ingest → blueprint → render chain.

Sketchfab “CC0” kits and parts (useful for kitbashing)

Sketchfab has CC0-tagged kits (like land vehicle kits) that can be helpful for placeholder geometry. But licenses are user-submitted and you’ll sometimes see confusing metadata, so treat it as “verify before shipping.”
Sketchfab

NASA imagery / models caution

NASA’s own media usage guidance explicitly says the NASA insignia/logotype/identifiers are protected and imagery is available under usage guidelines (so: don’t assume “everything NASA = public domain”).
NASA

That doesn’t mean “don’t use NASA sources”—it means “track provenance + follow rules,” which we’re going to formalize in v13 with a license/provenance manifest.

Here we go — Visual Blueprint Pack v10 (Effects) is done and ready to drop into your repo.



Download warbits_visual_blueprint_pack_v10_effects.zip



This pack is the missing “life” layer: tracers, contrails/smoke trails, explosions, and impact bursts, all designed to be wireframe/holographic, pooled, and hard-capped for uncapped FPS.



I’m also explicitly aligning these FX patterns to the way your Matplotlib prototype examples approach motion/terrain/overlay behavior.

matplotlibs examples

What this pack adds (v10)
1) Renderer-agnostic FX core (fast + deterministic)

New package:

warbits/visual/effects/

config.py → FxConfig caps + lifetimes (the “don’t tank FPS” knobs)

trails.py → TrailRingBuffer (pooled trails: tracers / contrails / smoke)

explosions.py → ExplosionPool (wireframe spheres that expand + fade)

bursts.py → BurstPool (impact “starburst splats” oriented to a normal)

manager.py → FxManager (one object you feed positions + events; it outputs a per-frame geometry batch)

types.py → FxFrameData batch container

Key design rule: the FX system outputs only:

line segments (N,2,3) in world space

alpha (N,) for fading
…and nothing renderer-specific.

So your Matplotlib version and Panda3D version both draw the exact same FX data.

2) Matplotlib FX layer (re-uses artists, updates segments)

New module:

warbits/visual/mpl/effects_layer.py → MplFxLayer

It creates (and keeps) one Line3DCollection per FX layer:

tracers

contrails

explosions

impacts

Per frame you call:

mpl_fx.update(fx_frame_data)

It updates segments + colors (alpha fade), without recreating artists.

3) Panda3D FX layer (uses your existing LineBatch for speed)

New module:

warbits/visual/panda3d/effects_layer.py → P3DFxLayer

It uses the already-existing LineBatch system from the Panda3D packs (so you get batching instead of “1 NodePath per line”, which would murder FPS).



Per frame you call:

p3d_fx.update(fx_frame_data)

How to integrate it (Matplotlib first)
Step 1 — Extract/merge

Unzip and merge into your repo root so these land in:

warbits/visual/effects/

warbits/visual/mpl/effects_layer.py

tests/test_visual_fx_*.py (optional but recommended)

Step 2 — Create an FxManager once

Somewhere in your Matplotlib renderer init (where you already create terrain + blueprint layers):

from warbits.visual.effects.config import FxConfig
from warbits.visual.effects.manager import FxManager
from warbits.visual.mpl.effects_layer import MplFxLayer

fx_cfg = FxConfig(
    max_tracer_objects=1200,
    max_tracer_segments=6000,
    max_contrail_objects=128,
    max_contrail_segments=4000,
    max_explosion_instances=128,
    max_impact_instances=256,
)

fx = FxManager(fx_cfg)
mpl_fx = MplFxLayer(ax, max_segments_per_layer=8000)


Those numbers are safe-ish defaults. You’ll tune them based on actual projectile counts.

Step 3 — Feed positions every frame (tracers + contrails)

Where your sim loop has access to live entity positions:

frame_idx += 1

# Bullets/cannon projectiles (ids + positions)
# ids: np.ndarray shape (B,), dtype int64
# pos: np.ndarray shape (B,3), float
fx.update_tracers(ids=bullet_ids, positions=bullet_positions, frame_idx=frame_idx)

# Aircraft contrails (ids + positions)
fx.update_contrails(ids=aircraft_ids, positions=aircraft_positions, frame_idx=frame_idx)


If you don’t have stable projectile IDs yet:

start with “slot ids” from your projectile buffer indices

stability matters because trails are tied to ids

Step 4 — Feed events (explosions, impacts)

Whenever your sim emits explosions/impacts, feed them as dicts:

fx.ingest_event_dicts(
    [
        {"type": "explosion", "pos": (x, y, z), "radius": 12.0, "life": 18},
        {"type": "impact", "pos": (ix, iy, iz), "radius": 3.0, "life": 10, "normal": (0,0,1)},
    ],
    frame_idx=frame_idx
)

Step 5 — Build + render the FX batch

At the end of your render step:

frame_data = fx.build_frame(frame_idx)
mpl_fx.update(frame_data)


That’s it. Now you have:

bullet tracers

contrails

wireframe explosions

impact bursts
…all in your same wireframe language.

Panda3D integration (later, same data)

Once you move to Panda3D, you keep FxManager exactly the same.



You swap only the layer:

from warbits.visual.panda3d.effects_layer import P3DFxLayer

p3d_fx = P3DFxLayer(parent_np=render)  # or whatever root node
...
frame_data = fx.build_frame(frame_idx)
p3d_fx.update(frame_data)


So the “FX brain” is shared; only the drawing backend changes.

Download warbits_visual_blueprint_pack_v11_hud_targeting.zip



This is Visual Blueprint Pack v11 — the HUD + Targeting layer. It’s built to be renderer-agnostic at the logic level, with fast overlay renderers for both Matplotlib and Panda3D.

What v11 adds (hardcore, practical, “War Thunder-ish” baseline)
1) A real targeting math core (deterministic + testable)

New module: warbits/visual/hud/targeting.py



It gives you:

Intercept lead solution (shooter → moving target) using the classic quadratic form:

handles “no solution” (target too fast / out-running projectile)

Gravity compensation (optional) so the pipper aims above at longer times-of-flight

Returns an AimSolution:

intercept time t

normalized aim direction

aimpoint in world-space

This is the brain that lets your HUD stop being “decorations” and start being truthy.

2) A renderer-agnostic HUD primitive system

New module: warbits/visual/hud/types.py



Defines:

HudLine, HudCircle, HudBox, HudText

HudTheme (color + thickness defaults)

HudContext (camera parameters, ownship, target list, weapon info)

So your sim can spit out “draw commands” without caring if the final renderer is Matplotlib or Panda3D.

3) Projection abstraction (so the HUD logic doesn’t marry one renderer)

New module: warbits/visual/hud/projector.py



Includes:

PinholeProjector (pure math, fast, works anywhere)

PinholeCamera (camera pose + fov + aspect)

This is key because:

Matplotlib’s 3D projection is weird.

Panda3D projection is correct and fast.

You still want one HUD builder.

So the builder talks to a ScreenProjector, not to Matplotlib/Panda3D directly.

4) A “HUD builder” that outputs primitives

New module: warbits/visual/hud/builder.py



Generates:

Center crosshair

Target box + label (range + ID)

Lead circle (pipper) from AimSolution

Optional “edge clamp” indicator: if the point is off-screen, it clamps to the screen edge so you still get directional info (you’ll feel this immediately in gameplay).

5) High-performance overlay renderers (don’t redraw everything every frame)
Matplotlib

New module: warbits/visual/mpl/hud_overlay.py

Builds a dedicated 2D overlay axes on top of your 3D axes.

Uses artist pooling:

Lines/texts/circles are reused, not recreated.

Designed so the expensive part is your 3D scene, not the HUD.

Panda3D

New module: warbits/visual/panda3d/hud_overlay.py

Uses a dynamic Geom line drawer (UHDynamic) so you can update points without rebuilding nodes constantly.

Text uses OnscreenText.

This is the path to “uncapped FPS” in the real runtime (Matplotlib will never truly be that; Panda3D can be).

6) Tests (so we don’t build a haunted house)

tests/test_visual_hud_targeting.py

tests/test_visual_hud_builder.py

They check:

intercept time is sane

gravity compensation moves the pipper the right direction

generated HUD primitives are stable and correct

What this pack adds (v12)

This one is purely about keeping visuals fast and scalable while you crank realism upward.

1) Visual performance harness (low-allocation)

New: warbits/visual/perf/

VisualPerf — fixed-stage frame timers (terrain/entities/projectiles/hud/effects/total) designed to avoid “dict-per-frame” garbage.

VisualBudget — tripwire budgets (not hard caps) so you catch FPS rot early.

2) Deterministic LOD policy (distance + projected size)

New: warbits/visual/lod/

CameraModel + projected_radius_px() — fast projection estimate that doesn’t need renderer imports.

LODPolicy — deterministic tier selector: HIGH / MED / LOW / ICON.

This is how you stop rendering 12,000 edges for a vehicle that’s 4 pixels tall.

3) Projectile batching primitive

New: warbits/visual/batch/

ProjectileSegmentBatch — preallocated (N,2,3) float32 segments buffer for “prev→curr” tracer-style motion lines (works as input for Matplotlib Line3DCollection or Panda3D line batches).

4) Panda3D dynamic resolution controller (renderer-agnostic)

New: warbits/visual/panda3d/dynres.py

DynamicResolutionScaler — adjusts a render_scale based on frame time (you wire it to your Panda3D RTT/pixel pipeline).

5) Tests + docs

Tests: tests/test_visual_*

Docs: docs/VISUAL_PERF_LOD_GUIDE.md + updated docs/VISUAL_SYSTEM_TRACKER.md
